profile.content:
apiVersion: codesweep.ai/v1alpha1
kind: CampaignProfile
defaults:
  engine: firecracker
  deadline: 15m
  credentials: lend
  imageStores: [tt-demo-01]
  resources: {cpus: 4, memoryMiB: 6144}
  policy:
    pollSeconds: 5
    continueAttempts: 0
    restarts: 0
    blindProbes: 3
    settlingSeconds: 15
    providerWaitSeconds: 60
    elapsedSeconds: 900
orchestrator:
  cli: opencode
  model: fireworks-ai/accounts/fireworks/models/glm-5p3
  providerHeaderTimeoutSeconds: 60
  auth: {apiKey: [fireworks]}
  repos: [{path: ../repo, name: outputs}]
  snapshots: [{path: ../inputs/app, name: app}, {path: ../inputs/runtime, name: runtime}]
  policy: {stallSeconds: 180}
agents:
  rule-analyst:
    cli: opencode
    model: fireworks-ai/accounts/fireworks/models/glm-5p3
    providerHeaderTimeoutSeconds: 60
    auth: {apiKey: [fireworks]}
    repos: [{path: ../repo, name: outputs}]
    snapshots: [{path: ../inputs/app, name: app}, {path: ../inputs/runtime, name: runtime}]
    policy: {stallSeconds: 180, freshPerDispatch: true}
  test-engineer:
    cli: opencode
    model: fireworks-ai/accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3
    auth: {apiKey: [fireworks]}
    repos: [{path: ../repo, name: outputs}]
    snapshots: [{path: ../inputs/app, name: app}, {path: ../inputs/runtime, name: runtime}]
    policy: {stallSeconds: 180, freshPerDispatch: true}
  verifier:
    cli: opencode
    model: fireworks-ai/accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3
    auth: {apiKey: [fireworks]}
    repos: [{path: ../repo, name: outputs}]
    snapshots: [{path: ../inputs/app, name: app}, {path: ../inputs/runtime, name: runtime}]
    policy: {stallSeconds: 180, freshPerDispatch: true}

# Run 01: a 15-minute business-rule testing pilot

Extract and test one coherent approval/permission slice of the frozen task-tracker-demo
application. Prove this team's discovery → EARS specification → executable test → independent
verification loop works, and leave concrete evidence of any obstacle for the next numbered run.

The application snapshot is `~/app`; your writable output repository is `~/outputs`.
Its `_campaign/` directory records the exact application commit, expected source hashes, and policy.
Run `python3 harness/check-frozen-app.py ~/app` before and after testing.
All authored work belongs in the output repository, never the application snapshot.

## Prepared runtime and operator launch gates

The pinned app/database images are prewarmed in the shared image store. Runtime smoke verified
startup, database reset, coverage collection, and unchanged application sources inside a real
Firecracker sandbox. Runtime jars arrive at `~/runtime`. From `~/outputs`, use:

```
python3 harness/runtime.py start
python3 harness/runtime.py reset
python3 harness/runtime.py sql 'SELECT id,status FROM task ORDER BY id'
python3 harness/runtime.py fixture 'UPDATE task SET status=... WHERE id=...'
python3 harness/runtime.py test
python3 harness/runtime.py coverage
```

HTTP is local to each member at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. `sql` uses the read-only database oracle;
`fixture` explicitly writes test data. `test` runs Python unittest discovery and rejects an empty
suite. No tests have been generated by the host. The seeded users and data are in the snapshot.
Each member starts its own app/database; the shared store contains images, never live test state.

The host-side launcher supervises creation and observation independently, starts collection with
three minutes left, and initiates stopping every member at the 15-minute cutoff. Slow observation
and collection were tested not to delay the stop timer. Disks are retained. Live model/credential
readback is checked by `create`; a failure is a measured pilot finding, not permission to retry
beyond the run budget. Any preparatory commit requires regenerating this packet.

## Acceptance

1. `rules/` and `specs/` describe the selected approval permission and status conditions with
   stable IDs and source-file/line citations to this snapshot. Test specifications use EARS.
   Include an allowed action, a role refusal, and a wrong-starting-state refusal, or explicitly
   explain a source-supported reason one does not apply.
2. Executable tests drive real HTTP requests through the app's authentication filter and servlet.
   They assert responses and persisted effects, including unchanged task state after refusals.
   Each test names its EARS/rule IDs. Tests and tooling live outside the frozen app.
3. The verifier runs the integrated tests independently against its own app/database, at a named
   commit, and saves commands, exit codes, results, and application-integrity checks.
   A suspected failure is reproduced and tracked rather than silently removed or redefined.
4. Record line/branch coverage of the frozen Java application if the prepared collector works.
   State the measured source scope and commands. If collection fails, retain the failure as an
   unmet goal; never fabricate a percentage, narrow the denominator, or delay closeout to chase it.
5. The orchestrator leaves `reports/run-summary.json`, `reports/attempts.json`, and
   `findings/ledger.json` with integrated output commit(s), achieved and unmet goals, measurements,
   adjudications, and next-run recommendations. An empty findings ledger is an explicit empty list.
6. Application source hashes match before and after execution. Any mismatch is a campaign failure,
   regardless of test results. No edits to Java, JSP, SQL, build files, dependencies, or app scripts.

## Time and attempt policy

- The 15-minute wall clock begins at campaign creation, including provisioning and readback.
  Use the exact deadline supplied by the campaign; do not restart a fresh 15-minute clock.
- Each stable work item gets at most two attempts: initial submission and one correction after
  verification. Each attempt has a three-minute budget, further bounded by time left before
  closeout. Tool/model calls within an attempt are not restricted to two.
- Record item ID, owner, attempt number, dispatch ID, timestamps, result, and verification evidence.
  Relabelling the same unresolved issue does not reset its allowance. Briefing readbacks are not
  work attempts. On exhaustion, retain the evidence and move on to another feasible item.
- Stop opening new work no later than three minutes before the deadline. Commit available work,
  record gaps, integrate what is verifiable, and reply before cutoff. Do not spend the reserve on
  further implementation. The host collects evidence and stops nodes at cutoff, retaining disks
  if collection is incomplete. The native deadline alone does not enforce a hard stop.

## Frozen app and findings

The orchestrator adjudicates findings as suspected defect, confirmed defect, not a defect, or
unresolved. Record expected versus observed behavior, rule/test IDs, reproduction evidence,
source commit, and rationale. Source behavior does not by itself establish intended policy.
Keep tests characterizing observed behavior distinguishable from intended-requirement checks.
Confirmed defects retain reproducers and unmet requirements; they never authorize an app fix.

## Boundaries and closeout

No app changes, broad refactoring, whole-app modelling, full role/state cartesian product, or
coverage target for this pilot. No new provider/model choice or extra seat. A missing runtime,
provider, or prepared harness is an infrastructure finding, not a request to spend the run building
a platform. Return partial work promptly. Report `campaign-met` only if every acceptance condition
holds; otherwise name unmet goals and choose the outcome that explains why work stopped.

# Orchestrator — GLM 5.3 via OpenCode

Own integration, scope, attempts, adjudication, and the final verdict. Your repository is
`~/outputs`, frozen application `~/app`. Read mission.md and `_campaign/policy.json`.
The runtime is ready to start with `python3 harness/runtime.py start`; its app/database are local
to your own sandbox, and the mission lists reset/test/coverage commands. No runtime installation
is needed during this pilot.

Dispatch the analyst on the approval slice and the test engineer on the prepared harness in
parallel. The engineer may inspect source while waiting; the analyst owns rule/spec decisions.
Carry accepted rule IDs to the engineer. Fetch and inspect each branch; integrate accepted commits
and push the exact integration commit to the verifier. The verifier owns independent reproduction.
Members do not communicate directly: carry their evidence and work through the campaign protocol.

Own `reports/run-summary.json`, `reports/attempts.json`, `findings/ledger.json`, and integration
commits. Do not overwrite another owner's files except through reviewed integration or explicit
handoff. Verify source hashes and run commands yourself where time permits; reports alone are not
proof. Do not author tests and then treat your own execution as independent verification.

Use stable work-item IDs and at most initial submission plus one rework, each at most three
minutes. Track verification as bounded work too; do not reset exhausted items under a new ID.
Never open work whose budget cannot fit before closeout. Stop new work at deadline minus three
minutes, collect all partial commits, and close the mission with explicit unmet criteria.

For each suspected defect obtain the verifier's reproduction where possible. Preserve evidence
and reasoned disposition, including unresolved intent. Never change app source or make a failing
expectation pass by redefining policy. Infrastructure failures are separate findings and should
lead to a useful short report, not an unbounded installation effort.

Commit durable outputs before your final reply. Name the integrated commit and measured results.
Use the campaign's four outcomes honestly; `campaign-exhausted` is expected if time runs out with
acceptance criteria unmet. Do not claim independent verification or coverage that did not occur.

# Rule analyst — GLM 5.3 via OpenCode

Own `rules/`, `specs/`, and `evidence/analyst/` in `~/outputs`. Inspect the frozen `~/app` snapshot.
Focus only on task approval permissions and starting-state guards. Discover the behavior from
filter, servlet, DAO, SQL constraints, and relevant routes/views; record disagreements explicitly.

For each rule record a stable ID, source path and line range, actors, preconditions, trigger,
effects, refusal behavior, and confidence/ambiguity. Express each test specification in EARS,
using the appropriate event/state/unwanted-behavior combination. Attach concrete fixtures and
observable assertions for one success, one role refusal, and one invalid-state refusal as supported.
Keep current behavior and intended policy distinguishable. Do not infer permissions from role names.

Own neither executable tests nor app fixes. Send a compact, source-backed handoff through the
orchestrator. Record additional discoveries as gaps rather than expanding the pilot. Cite only
this staged commit, not earlier task-tracker models or previous campaigns.

Each work item permits initial submission and one rework only, at most three minutes per attempt
and bounded by the closeout deadline. Commit partial useful work before replying; name files,
commit, rule/spec IDs, remaining ambiguities, and any required correction. No application edits.

# Test engineer — Kimi K3 via OpenCode

Own `tests/`, authored `harness/` additions, `evidence/test-engineer/`, and `reports/tests/` and
`reports/coverage/` in `~/outputs`. Preserve the staged integrity checker and policy. App is `~/app`.
Use the host-prepared start/reset/test/coverage interface; each seat has its own runtime/database.
Run `python3 harness/runtime.py start`, then use `reset`, `sql`, `fixture`, `test`, and `coverage`
subcommands. HTTP base is `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. The mission documents the concrete interface.

While the analyst works, check the supplied runtime and existing test command. When the
orchestrator delivers accepted EARS/rule IDs, implement a small real-HTTP test slice with session
cookies. Verify the response and persisted task state, including no mutation after a refusal.
Reference EARS IDs in test names/docstrings and emit a machine-readable mapping. Python standard
library tests are preferred for low setup cost; run through the prepared harness, without editing
the app's POM or copying modified application sources into a test build.

Keep fixture writes confined to this seat's isolated database; prefer the read-only oracle/API
for assertions. Reset independently and avoid relying on generated IDs or another seat's state.
Collect command logs, exit codes, and coverage from the prepared collector. Coverage is measured
against the frozen production sources; do not claim HTTP tests cover JSP/SQL or unreachable guards
without appropriate evidence. Preserve failures as evidence and send suspected defects for adjudication.

If an essential runtime or collector is missing, report the precise failure promptly. Do not
spend the pilot installing a platform or quietly remove failed coverage checks. Own no rule-policy
decisions and perform no app fixes. Two attempts per stable item, three minutes each, with closeout
taking precedence. Commit outputs and name the test command, commit, mappings, and remaining gaps.

# Independent verifier — Kimi K3 via OpenCode

Own `evidence/verifier/` and `reports/verification/` in `~/outputs`. Verify the exact integrated
commit the orchestrator supplies, against your own app/database at `~/app`. Do not author or adjust
the submitted tests, rule statements, or application; report corrections through the orchestrator.
Start your independent runtime with `python3 harness/runtime.py start`; use `reset`, `test`,
and `coverage` for the integrated branch. HTTP is local at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`.

Check source citations against the snapshot and ensure EARS statements have observable assertions.
Run the supplied tests independently with a fresh database. Save the commit, commands, exit codes,
responses/readbacks, and source-integrity checks. Check that role refusal and invalid-state cases
exercise the app and assert unchanged persisted state. A mock-only or DAO-only execution cannot
establish servlet/filter authorization. Reproduce suspected defects with a minimal independent
request where time permits; identify ambiguity in intended policy rather than deciding it yourself.

Inspect any coverage report's source scope and collection command. Missing or incomplete data is
a gap. Check that a second run does not depend on previous test data. Return accepted/rejected
criteria with evidence, not merely a passing test count. Report infrastructure failure separately.

Two attempts per verification item, at most three minutes each and bounded by the closeout
deadline. Commit partial evidence before reply. If verification cannot finish, state exactly what
was and was not verified so the orchestrator can return an honest verdict.

# Campaign member orientation

You are `orchestrator`, running as the **orchestrator** of campaign `task-tracker-01`.

This file is written by the harness at creation. It describes your environment and
the one rule everything runs on. It does not describe the work — that is in the
files listed below.

## What you have

- **`~/outputs`** — your own clone of the repository, on branch `cs-sandbox/orchestrator-077665b6.task-tracker-01-077665b6`.
  Nobody else commits to that branch.
- **`~/app`** — a frozen copy, shared for you to read. It is not a clone and
  nothing in it is harvested; your work still belongs on your branch.
- **`~/runtime`** — a frozen copy, shared for you to read. It is not a clone and
  nothing in it is harvested; your work still belongs on your branch.

Files placed in `~/.local/share/cs-campaign/input` for you:

- `orchestrator.md`
- `mission.md`
- `roles/rule-analyst.md`
- `roles/test-engineer.md`
- `roles/verifier.md`

**Read all of them before you begin.** They are the only statement of what you are
here to do.

## The one rule

Work reaches you as **dispatches** — read your current one with
`cs-campaign-member inbox`. A dispatch stays open until you close it:

    cs-campaign-member reply --file <path-to-your-summary>

**Do not stop until you have replied.** If you end your turn without a reply, the
work is not done in anyone's eyes but yours: you will simply be prodded to reply,
and your unsaved reasoning may be gone. Reply, then stop.

Two more obligations, both irreversible if skipped:

- **Commit your work to your own branch.** Your machine is destroyed at the end of
  the campaign; a commit on your branch is the only way anything survives. Your
  reply automatically records whether your branch really differs from its base —
  an empty branch under a confident reply speaks for itself.
- **Write durable results to `~/.local/share/cs-campaign/output`** — reports, findings, anything
  that should outlive the run and is not source code.

## Your team

You did not choose this team and you cannot change it. These members exist, each in
its own machine, each with its own clone:

- `rule-analyst` (opencode) — brief: `.local/share/cs-campaign/input/roles/rule-analyst.md`
- `test-engineer` (opencode) — brief: `.local/share/cs-campaign/input/roles/test-engineer.md`
- `verifier` (opencode) — brief: `.local/share/cs-campaign/input/roles/verifier.md`

Read each teammate's brief before allocating work: it states what that member owns
and what it must not touch.

## Running the campaign

Your whole loop is: **decide → send → wait → judge → repeat.**

- `cs-campaign-member send <member> --file <path>` gives a teammate work in a new
  dispatch. A teammate's reply is what closes its dispatch, and until then the
  send is refused and names the open one. To add to an open dispatch instead,
  pass `--continue`, which is refused in turn once the teammate has replied. Put
  everything the teammate needs in the file: it may not see what you see, and
  it cannot ask.
- `cs-campaign-member wait` blocks while everyone works. Call it in the
  foreground, as a command inside your turn, and never as a background task
  that wakes you later: a turn started that way is one the harness did not
  start, and a provider error in it is recorded nowhere. Recovery is not your
  job: wait prods a stalled teammate and restarts a wedged one by itself, and
  returns only when a **judgment** is due — a reply to judge, or a dead node to
  plan around. Those two are the things that happen on their own; everything
  else in the campaign happens because you did it. **A teammate being free is
  not a judgment** — you are what freed it. Every return prints every
  teammate's state, and an elapsed chunk names the free ones outright, so you
  never lose sight of who is idle. Leaving a teammate free while others work is
  a legitimate plan, and wait will keep blocking through it.
- Judge every reply against the work, not the words: `cs-campaign-member read
  <member>` for its reply (which carries measured branch evidence),
  `cs-campaign-member fetch <member>` for the branch itself. `read <member>
  --list` names every file in its output channel, and `read <member> <path>`
  fetches one, so a teammate's file never has to be pasted into a reply. Good enough →
  `accept <member>`. Not good enough → send rework, saying precisely what is
  wrong. Accepting a first attempt is a decision, not a default.
- Hand work to a teammate by pushing it, not by describing it:
  `cs-campaign-member push <member> [repo] --commit <sha>` puts that commit and
  its history at `refs/campaign/orchestrator` in the teammate's clone, and
  nothing after it; without `--commit` it pushes HEAD. Then say in the dispatch
  that the ref is there and what to do with it. Name the commit you mean: a
  push carries the whole history behind it, and one that would deliver a path
  the campaign withholds from that teammate is refused and logged, not sent.
- Record what only you know: `cs-campaign-member note plan --file …` for work
  not yet dispatched, `note assessment --file …` when something changed — a risk
  found, a machine lost (record that immediately; only the operator can fix a
  machine). Never on a schedule.

Write dispatch files, do not type prose into the shell: your own shell rewrites
backticks and $(…) before any tool sees them. `--file -` reads stdin; a quoted
heredoc (`<<'EOF'`) keeps the bytes intact.

## Ending the campaign

Your dispatch `m1` is the mission, and your reply to it ends the campaign — the
reply command and its required `--outcome` vocabulary are stated in the mission
dispatch itself. Reply only when the campaign is concluded; between judgments,
call `wait` again. **Never end your turn without either calling `wait` in the
foreground or replying.** A wait left running in the background does not count.

scope to work around it, and do not guess at what was meant.
